findings.severity: requirement discovered — actionable, and only visible because the round trip was performed
findings.title: A receiving daemon’s displayed image id is not a sound identity check; the config-object hash is.
findings.statement: Loading the verified archive on Docker 29.5.3 with the containerd image store (Driver=overlayfs, io.containerd.snapshotter.v1) produced image ID sha256:180e4a3dc31da6f0... — NOT the bound sha256:770553aeae6c... The CONTENT is identical: all eight RootFS layer diff IDs match the source exactly, and the Created timestamp matches to the nanosecond (2026-07-13T23:39:13.458225455Z). The daemon assigns its own identifier under that store.
findings.why_this_matters: The owner required the load round trip precisely because a SHA-256 over the tar is transport custody and not the governed runtime identity. The round trip earned its keep — but for a different reason than first written: it showed that a receiving daemon's DISPLAYED id is not a sound identity check, which is itself worth knowing before any future environment relies on one.

WITHDRAWN_requirement.what_was_written: an earlier draft of this record concluded that the reproduction environment MUST run a classic (non-containerd) image store so that `docker load` restores the id as sha256:770553ae...
WITHDRAWN_requirement.status: WITHDRAWN before this record was first committed, on owner ruling 2026-08-21
WITHDRAWN_requirement.why_it_was_wrong: It treated the receiving daemon's displayed id as the governed identity. It is not. The Docker image specification defines image identity as the SHA-256 of the image CONFIGURATION JSON, and that object has already been independently hashed out of the archive to exactly sha256:770553ae... Moby additionally documents that under the containerd image store the IMAGE ID field may display a manifest/index digest rather than the config digest, and Docker describes the classic store as a compatibility option for older behaviour. So 180e4a3d... is a display artefact of the receiving store, not a different runtime.
WITHDRAWN_requirement.why_the_withdrawal_matters_practically: Provisioning a classic-store host to make a daemon PRINT a historical value would introduce an unnecessary variable into a numerical-reproduction environment in order to satisfy a cosmetic check. That is the opposite of what runtime pinning is for.

findings.revised_requirement_condition_1: Condition 1 is satisfied by CRYPTOGRAPHIC CONTENT IDENTITY, not by a receiving daemon's displayed id. The governed check is: extract the config object from the archive, hash it, and require sha256:770553aeae6c... ; additionally require the eight layer DiffIDs and the creation metadata to match. All three hold. This check is store-independent, daemon-independent, and performable by anyone holding the archive.
findings.residual_note_for_any_future_numerical_h: If a numerical run is ever authorized, matching the evaluator host's daemon configuration is a defensible conservative choice on general reproducibility grounds — but it is NOT required for numerical determinism (the image store does not influence BLAS kernel selection or floating-point behaviour) and it must never be adopted merely to reproduce a displayed identifier.

two_identities_recorded_not_conflated.rule: these are not the same identifier and must never be written as if they were, in either direction

findings.severity: verification hazard — corrects a sharper alarm the developer raised and then disproved
findings.title: The image ID is unstable across daemons; the tag mr002-research:v1.4 resolves differently on different machines.
findings.statement: The workstation already carried an image tagged mr002-research:v1.4 with ID sha256:aa930021c072... A first reading suggested a look-alike substitution. It is NOT one: the full eight-layer diff-ID set is IDENTICAL to the bound image and the Created timestamp matches exactly. It is the same content under a different daemon-assigned ID, the same effect as P1-PRES-F1.
findings.corrected_characterisation: This is a VERIFICATION hazard, not a substitution hazard in this instance. But the operational consequence still favours the owner's condition: resolving or verifying by tag OR by image ID on a containerd-store daemon can disagree with the binding while the content is correct — and could equally agree by accident while the content is wrong. Only the config blob's own content hash settles it.
findings.practical_rule: verify the config blob's sha256 out of the archive, which is store-independent, and additionally require the classic-store load to reproduce the bound ID before any governed numerical run.

findings.severity: refinement of a committed finding — additive, T2b not rewritten
findings.title: A second copy of the image already existed on the same volume; F4's substance is unchanged, its wording was imprecise.
findings.statement: T2b said the runtime 'existed as a SINGLE local Docker image on one stopped EBS volume.' There were in fact TWO copies, both on that same volume: the daemon's image store, and /opt/mr002/runtime_custody/mr002-research-v14.tar (142,534,656 bytes, sha256 95076c14b32bee01a54e2d49a9a42bea47ef9c73ffb5c0a998c7a10d174c346e, dated 2026-08-18), whose manifest.json names Config blobs/sha256/770553aeae6c... and RepoTags [mr002-research:v1.4].
findings.why_the_finding_survives: Two copies on ONE volume is one point of failure, not two. There was no registry copy, no off-host copy, and no custody record covering either. Loss of that volume would still have made exact runtime reproduction impossible. F4 stands; only the count was wrong.
findings.note_on_the_two_archives: The 08-18 archive (142,534,656 bytes) and today's export (432,910,336 bytes) have different sizes and different tar hashes while naming the same config digest — a direct illustration of why the tar hash is transport custody and the config blob is identity.
